name: Geko Karen
world_status: a description exists but is not accessible

sources.citation: Shintani, Tadahiko L. A. 2025. Kayan-kei gengo no bunrui [Classification of Kayan languages]. In Sawada Hideo (ed.), Toward construction of a typological and genetic overview of minority languages in Burma, 135-146. Tokyo: ILCAA. doi 10.15026/0002001132
sources.note: Japanese; says the former 'Pado-Thaido-Gekho' group (2003 classification) has since been surveyed and published in the LSTCA series; tone system only; no stress; reference list gives LSTCA 106 Kadaw, 116 Thaidai (not 111 Gokhu).

sources.citation: Kato, Atsuhiko. 2021. Typological profile of Karenic languages. In P. Sidwell & M. Jenny (eds.), The Languages and Linguistics of Mainland Southeast Asia, ch. 18. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton.
sources.note: Family-level only: after describing Eastern Pwo sesquisyllables as 'composed of the unstressed first syllable and the stressed second syllable', says 'Karenic languages generally have sesquisyllabic words' (with Kayah Li and Kayan examples from Solnit 1997 and Manson 2010). Gek(h)o appears only in the ethnic-group list and in a negation-typology list; no Geko-specific statement.

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.3 languoid page geko1235 (names, classification per Ken Manson 2019) and langdoc page
sources.note: Bibliographic only; alternative names include Padaung and Kekaungdu, which explains why Khammuang 1998 (Padaung) is attached to this code; the refs table is JS-loaded and empty in the saved HTML ( endpoint returns 406).

sources.citation: van der Hulst, Harry, Rob Goedemans & Ellen van Zanten (eds.). 2010. A Survey of Word Accentual Patterns in the Languages of the World, ch. on Asia (StressTyp).
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: online with a university library login (also: harvard online access (harvardkey); publisher (doi, likely paywalled))
sources.note: 'UNCLASSIFIED: Bwe Karen, Geko Karen' appears only in the Tibeto-Burman classification list; no datum for Geko.

sources.citation: Manson, Ken. 2009. Prolegomena to reconstructing Proto-Karen. La Trobe Papers in Linguistics 12. 26 pp. doi 10.26181/22202458.v1
sources.note: Areal remark only (sec. 5.2): 'Most languages of Southeast Asia are sesquisyllabic (i.e. they have iambic stress)'; Gheko appears only in the Kauffman-derived classification tree (fig. 6).

sources.citation: Wikipedia. Geko Karen language (accessed 2026-09-17)
sources.note: Dialects Geker, Gekho, Thaidai (Htideh); Yinbaw reportedly a variety; Kadaw and Taungmying closely related; cites Shintani 2015 Kadaw (LSTCA 106), 2017 Gokhu (LSTCA 111), 2018 Thaidai (LSTCA 116), 2012 Brakaloungic handbook; no phonology.

sources.citation: Wikipedia. Kayan people (Myanmar) (accessed 2026-09-17)
sources.note: Lists 'Kayan Ka Khaung (Gekho)' among Kayan subgroups and Padaung as the Shan term for Kayan Lahwi; no language data.

sources.citation: Hsiu, Andrew. 2019. Karenic. Sino-Tibetan Branches Project (sites.google.com/site/sinotibetanbranches/eastern-sino-tibetan/karenic)
sources.note: Classification only (Gekho cluster = Gekho, Kadaw, Taungmying; Thaidai separate; follows Shintani 2012); cites only Shintani 2012 and Luangthongkum 2019; nothing on phonology.

sources.citation: Luangthongkum, Theraphan. 2019. A View on Proto-Karen Phonology and Lexicon. JSEALS 12.1: i-lii. hdl 10524/52441
sources.note: Geko only in the list of 16 Karen groups of Myanmar; no Geko data; nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Manson, Ken. 2019. Kayan dialects in light of Proto-Karen. Handout, 52nd ICSTLL, University of Sydney. 10 pp. doi 10.26181/5fced5d04e826
sources.note: Only first-hand Geko data opened: Gekho [ghk] is one of 5 Kayan-cluster languages, 5 Gekho doculects, Proto-Gekho tone box, tone-table rows Gekho (TS), Gekho Y (TS), Kadaw (TS); notes 'Variation in articulation/intonation (staccato, flowing stream)' for the cluster; tones and segments only, nothing on stress/accent.

sources.citation: Ywar, Naw Hsa Eh. 2013. A grammar of Kayan Lahta. MA thesis, Payap University. xiii+175 pp.
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: not located online or in the libraries checked
sources.note: Kekhu appears only in the Karenic classification tree (thesis p. 3); different language (Lahta); no stress statement in the thesis.

sources.citation: Manson, Ken. 2011. The subgrouping of Karen. Paper + handouts, SEALS 21, Bangkok.
sources.note: Geker and Gekho rhyme/tone developments and a 'Geko (Km)' column in sound-change tables; nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Kauffman, William G. 1993. The Great Tone Split and Central Karen. MA thesis, University of North Dakota. 124 pp.
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: online with a university library login (also: harvard online access (harvardkey))
sources.note: Gheko only in the classification tree (p. 5) and one ethnographic aside; the Padaung (Kayan Lahwi) sketch sec. 2.3 mentions reduced vowels 'in unstressed syllables' with no placement rule; no Geko data.

sources.citation: Scott, J. George & J. P. Hardiman. 1900. Gazetteer of Upper Burma and the Shan States, Part I, Vol. I, ch. IX Ethnology. Rangoon: Government Printing.
sources.note: p. 530: 'The Padaungs or Kekawngdu'; 'Keku Karens... speaking a dialect of Karen' -- ethnography only, no language description.
